title: Ben Chiriboga (Nexl) on Legal Tech, Innovation, and the Future of Law
author: Ben Chiriboga

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: The source does not assess agentic delegation, autonomy levels, error propagation or verification bottlenecks. Instead, it redirects attention from workflow augmentation toward a speculative long-term thesis: AI’s principal legal impact will be the creation of new law-firm jobs, roles and outputs, while lawyers retain trusted strategic-adviser relationships.
qs: At the end of the day, AI is largely about the jobs and the roles that is going to be created.

And truthfully, I think when we look back 40 years from now, it will not be that there was a better drafted motion or even the something like the processual sort of like augmentation that led to maybe deeper or better or quicker service and work product.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Chiriboga shifts the focus from AI’s threat to apprenticeship and expertise reproduction toward AI-created roles, trusted-advisor relationships, competitive disruption and law-firm restructuring. He does not substantively address the verification paradox or the proposed reconstruction of associate training.
qs: At the end of the day, AI is largely about the jobs and the roles that is going to be created.

st.t: Civil justice: Capacity gains need human safeguards
st.an: The source’s host-level framing is compatible with human augmentation rather than replacement, but the excerpt does not address civil unmet need, bounded self-help, capacity expansion, verification, or other safeguards central to the cluster. Chiriboga’s own remarks are principally retrospective career and technology-adoption testimony, so there is insufficient evidence of his position on the cluster proposition.
qs: As he's going to tell us, it's not about replacing humans with AI, but about them using tech to give us superpowers.
It's about building a better relationship and a deeper connection with clients.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s human-augmentation orientation and notes early NLP use in e-discovery, but it does not address whether legal-specific workflow layers defend specialist value, require lawyer–engineer collaboration, or operate through verification and professional accountability. The evidence is therefore insufficient to determine its position on the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: As he's going to tell us, it's not about replacing humans with AI, but about them using tech to give us superpowers.
And for just a twist of fate, we end up getting this like e-discovery vendor and that has some early natural language processing basically in it.

st.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence
st.an: The excerpt contains only an invitation for legal-industry participants to share their stories and contact Chiriboga. It offers no substantive view on pragmatic AI adoption, experimentation, transformation evidence, or forecast autonomous workflows.
qs: So if that's like your jam, I'd love to talk to you and if you're in the legal industry and like want to rap about that, I would love to hear your story on my podcast.
And then if you don't email me and you can't find me, just hit me up on LinkedIn.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Chiriboga accepts the cluster’s core view that AI’s significance lies in organisational and production changes rather than technical capability alone. He materially extends it by forecasting that new law-firm jobs, roles and outputs will be more consequential than incremental augmentation, while reinforcing the cluster’s emphasis on durable strategic judgment and client relationships. These claims are explicitly exploratory predictions, not empirical findings.
qs: It's like, I'm going to make the claim that basically AI is not about the technology.
At the end of the day, AI is largely about the jobs and the roles that is going to be created.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Chiriboga broadly supports the synthesis’s view that AI will reshape legal delivery without eliminating the lawyer’s judgment and client-facing role. His prediction that AI will create new law-firm roles and outputs also aligns with work reallocation and demand expansion, but it remains exploratory and does not substantively address pricing pressure, apprenticeship, verification or implementation economics.
qs: So, you know, what's fundamental is the relationship.
At the end of the day, AI is largely about the jobs and the roles that is going to be created.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Chiriboga supports the cluster’s framing of AI as an operating-model and career-development challenge rather than straightforward lawyer substitution. He expects trusted strategic advice to remain human and predicts new law-firm roles and output, but offers this as a thesis to test without specifying roles or supplying evidence, so he does not materially extend the synthesis.
qs: So, you know, what's fundamental is the relationship.

But ultimately, what's really interesting is within the context of the law firm, what are the jobs that are going to come out of it that basically is facilitated with this kind of like capacity and technology.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s lawyer-guided augmentation framing by presenting AI as enhancing human capabilities and client relationships rather than replacing lawyers. Its support is limited to introductory framing and does not substantively address contextual agents, workflow redesign, integration or verification.
qs: As he's going to tell us, it's not about replacing humans with AI, but about them using tech to give us superpowers.
It's about building a better relationship and a deeper connection with clients.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Chiriboga supports the proposition that AI will reorganise legal-service production and provider structures rather than eliminate lawyers. He distinguishes automatable paperwork from relationship-intensive counselling and judgment, and predicts technology-led providers with lawyers in the loop, while presenting the scale and timing of disruption as speculative.
qs: It can automate all the paperwork, probably everything you need to do legally to go to court, but it can't automate that.
And there's this law firm that basically is coming out and saying like straight up, like we're a tech company that just happens to have lawyers in the loop.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core complementarity proposition: AI may transform legal work and generate new roles and outputs while preserving lawyers’ relationship-based strategic judgment. Its employment claims are explicitly forward-looking and unsupported by concrete role definitions or evidence, consistent with the cluster’s treatment of staffing outcomes as uncertain rather than established.
qs: So, you know, what's fundamental is the relationship.
At the end of the day, AI is largely about the jobs and the roles that is going to be created.

st.t: Technology delivery: Routine relief creates strategic capacity
st.an: The source supports technology-enabled legal delivery as a way to handle resource-intensive work through a combination of technology, legal professionals, project management and human oversight. However, its efficiency and cost claims are promotional and provide no measured evidence that freed capacity produces strategic work.
qs: By combining legal expertise and technology, Percipient enables legal teams to get more work done for less.
Our team of legal professionals leveraged tech and project management principles with the right amount of human oversight to deliver precise, efficient and cost-effective legal solutions.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Chiriboga supports the cluster’s core view that AI will automate selected routine legal tasks while shifting lawyers toward contextual judgment, strategy and trusted relationships. His speculation that some non-relational procedural services may become human-free is consistent with the cluster’s bounded-substitution caveat, though he provides little evidence on verification or measured capability limits.
qs: And what I think is not only are the best lawyers going to use AI to deliver, yes, great work product, but also contextualize sort of the state of the legal world and even arguably maybe like the business for these clients and do it in a way that is highly personalized.
This non-relationship stuff that we talked about, they're probably going to realize that maybe we just really don't need a human.

kp.k: Early NLP discovery demonstrated dramatic efficiency gains
kp.d: Chiriboga recalls that, around 2015–2016, an NLP-enabled e-discovery tool performed in approximately six hours work he had been unable to complete in six months on a product liability case. This is a personal retrospective account, not a measured productivity study or evidence about current generative AI.
qs: So this is like 2015, 2015, 2016.
It was like a product liability case and comes in and does in like six hours. What I hadn't been able to do in like six months

kp.k: Established client relationships muted incentives for technological change
kp.d: Asked by Main whether billing incentives or technology aversion explained colleagues' indifference, Chiriboga instead emphasizes the boutique maritime firm's culture, deep niche expertise and recurring clients. He describes technology as an efficiency measure for unusually large cases rather than central to the firm's identity; he does not establish foregone billable hours as the explanation.
qs: effectively, the bread and butter of this practice, which was just deep industry expertise, these deep niche practices, good clients that came for us over and over again
It's like at the end of the day, the clients are still going to come in.

kp.k: Legal-tech careers require commercial skills beyond legal expertise
kp.d: Drawing on his attempted transition through outside general counsel services, Chiriboga argues that early-stage legal-tech companies primarily need revenue generation and product building. He describes learning sales, marketing, growth and product skills because serving startups as counsel did not readily translate into an operational growth role.
qs: it's such a big jump from general counsel to kind of being a growth contributor in what early stage companies want
basically you need sales marketing people, you need people with deep networks and you need people to build it
I have to make this transition into sales, marketing, growth, product, something.

kp.k: Legal CRM adoption depends on removing manual-entry burdens
kp.d: Chiriboga argues that conventional CRM systems assume sales managers, meetings and incentives that law firms lack. He describes Nexl's approach as passively collecting interaction information from tools such as Outlook, enriching it with third-party data and generating insights, reversing the expectation that lawyers must continually enter and retrieve data. These are the vendor executive's account of the product and adoption mechanism, not independently evaluated outcomes.
qs: there is zero incentives for anybody to put anything into a CRM, let alone collaborate with each other in terms of doing business development
most of the information that lawyers would need to put in in any other CRM is largely passively grabbed and also enriched
It's enriching with third-party data.
we're delivering a system that's giving them information, giving them what we call relationship intelligence out to them.

kp.k: Trusted relationships remain fundamental despite task automation
kp.d: Chiriboga argues that much legal work is already templated or routine, but clients still seek contextual understanding and a trusted adviser. Using physical therapy as an analogy for human accountability and personalized guidance, he predicts that the best lawyers will use AI to improve work product and contextualize legal and business developments for individual clients. His account frames AI principally as augmentation of this relational role.
qs: a lot of it has gotten to a point of templatation and a lot of it has come to the roteness of it
a client is also coming to you as a trusted advisor, as a smart person that's sort of sitting in their corner

the best lawyers going to use AI to deliver, yes, great work product, but also contextualize sort of the state of the legal world and even arguably maybe like the business for these clients and do it in a way that is highly personalized

kp.k: Host distinguishes automatable paperwork from relational and strategic work
kp.d: Main proposes that AI will particularly affect the 'middle types of law,' while relationships remain important in family and other personal matters, jury advocacy and high-end corporate strategy. He separates potentially automatable paperwork and court preparation from hearing a client's story or advising on consequential choices. These are the host's hypotheses rather than demonstrated task boundaries.
qs: what I think it AI changes and impacts is kind of the middle types of law
It can automate all the paperwork, probably everything you need to do legally to go to court, but it can't automate that.
the high end corporate legal work where you need strategy, right? And the trusted advisor

kp.k: AI's lasting impact may be new legal-adjacent roles
kp.d: Chiriboga speculates that, looking back 40 years later, AI's principal legacy will be new jobs, roles and law-firm outputs rather than better motions or faster service alone. He emphasizes legal-adjacent and 'legal plus' careers, without specifying occupational counts, staffing ratios or evidence of net employment effects.
qs: At the end of the day, AI is largely about the jobs and the roles that is going to be created.
I think when we look back 40 years from now, it will not be that there was a better drafted motion
I think it's going to be, where did these jobs come from?
it's this world of like legal adjacent, legal plus

kp.k: Data and emotional intelligence complement AI-driven change
kp.d: Asked about non-AI technologies, Chiriboga identifies interaction-data aggregation, manipulation, characterization and analytics as underappreciated in legal services. He also broadens 'technology' metaphorically to include emotional intelligence and 'psychotechnologies' that help people see differently; this is a conceptual framing, not a tested intervention.
qs: the aggregation and the manipulation and the characterization of data as it relates to sort of like all the interactions. It's underappreciated today within legal.
I would say that emotional intelligence is basically a type of technology
they're ways to kind of like get yourself to see things a little bit differently.

kp.k: Ownership reform forecast depends on law-firm competitive pressure
kp.d: Main quotes Chiriboga's forecast that by 2030 ownership rules could change, non-lawyer specialists could receive equity, and workflow-based 'legal plus' units could replace lawyer/non-lawyer hierarchies. Chiriboga confirms that the timing rests principally on law firms driving reform after losing market share. He explicitly says he does not know how reform would occur, and Main challenges the claim that firms themselves will initiate it.
qs: Legal plus business units emerge, structure on business workflows, not lawyer, non-lawyer hierarchies.
I really don't know the how because things are so murky right now.
The 2030 thing is based principally on that thing that law firms basically drive the change.
It's because I think something about the market demand starts to slip away from them.

kp.k: AI-native providers could change competition and talent incentives
kp.d: Chiriboga predicts that operationally technology-led businesses presented as law firms could capture substantial market share. He contrasts their potential with Axiom and an earlier venture associated with Justin Khan, arguing that generative AI and falling model costs could enable a different cost structure. He links incumbent responses to needing equity upside to attract engineers, while acknowledging that he has not investigated the licensing arrangements of the provider he mentions.
qs: Very smart people put together law firm and name only, but tech company and operations, and they go after market share
Axiom didn't have ChatGPT, didn't have generative AI across those models, with prices going sort of down in terms of running these models.
Somebody is going to nail it. Somebody is going to understand how to do it. It starts to eat into market share in a very significant way.
there's no way in hell that the best engineers in the world are going to come work at a law firm unless they have tremendous upside.

kp.k: Host proposes regulatory confrontation as an alternative catalyst
kp.d: Main speculates that entrants may follow an Uber-like strategy of launching services first and confronting regulators later, potentially with or without lawyers. Chiriboga sees a related route in businesses calling themselves law firms while operating differently. The discussion describes possible market strategies, not an established legal authorization or a documented regulatory outcome.
qs: I think there's going to be companies out there, may involve lawyers, may not.
we're going to build something, F it, we're going to ask them for forgiveness later.
I think that might happen in law.
we just call it a law firm and then we just don't run it at all as a law firm

kp.k: Routine services may shift toward reduced human involvement
kp.d: Main suggests that clients may conclude that non-relational tasks, such as completing and submitting a form, do not need a human. Chiriboga tentatively agrees and predicts changing risk tolerance as buyers weigh imperfect outputs against price, speed and service experience. He argues that malpractice concerns drive excessive risk aversion and notes that human work is also imperfect, but supplies no comparative error-rate or safety evidence.
qs: This non-relationship stuff that we talked about, they're probably going to realize that maybe we just really don't need a human.
I just need this form filled out. Give it to whatever governing body you need to give it to and it solves the problem, right?
malpractice looms so heavy over the legal profession because and which drives them to this over indexing toward risk.
I know that the models aren't perfect. Everybody gets that.
I just think that whole risk tolerance changes fundamentally.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Ben Chiriboga reports that an early natural-language-processing discovery tool accomplished in roughly six hours work he had been unable to complete in six months.
pts.d: This is a retrospective account of discovery in a large product-liability case at his former boutique practice, not a measured general productivity estimate for AI or generative AI. He describes the experience as the catalyst for his move into legal technology.

pts.k: Chiriboga says Nexl combines passive relationship-data collection, third-party enrichment and generative AI to deliver insights to lawyers rather than requiring them to maintain a conventional CRM.
pts.d: He presents this as an existing product capability addressing law firms' lack of the incentives, managers and routines that support CRM data entry in sales organisations. Passive collection and enrichment are distinct from the generative-AI insight layer; he does not claim that AI performs all of these functions. Nexl is a software vendor, not a provider of legal work.

pts.k: Chiriboga predicts that the best lawyers will use AI to improve work product and provide highly personalised advice, while the trusted human relationship remains fundamental.
pts.d: His central framing is augmentation: lawyers use AI while continuing to interpret a client's circumstances, contextualise legal and business developments, and act as trusted advisers. He contrasts increasingly templated, routine work with the application of law to a person's life. His physical-therapy analogy illustrates the relational value he believes information and AI-generated plans cannot replace.

pts.k: Chiriboga predicts that AI's most important long-run legacy will be new legal-adjacent jobs, roles and law-firm outputs, rather than merely better or faster documents.
pts.d: He expects new professional opportunities enabled by AI capacity, describing them as 'legal adjacent' and 'legal plus'. He does not specify job counts, a net employment effect, or a detailed list of the roles that will emerge.

pts.k: Chiriboga predicts that operationally technology-led legal providers will use generative AI and falling model costs to win significant market share.
pts.d: He envisages businesses that retain the law-firm label but operate as technology companies. He argues that earlier ventures, including Axiom and the venture he associates with Justin Khan, did not have today's generative AI or declining model-running costs. His proposed mechanism is a less labour-intensive cost base, not an established finding that any named entrant has already achieved the predicted disruption. He mentions an unnamed tech-forward firm but expressly says he has not investigated its licensing arrangements.

pts.k: Chiriboga predicts that competitive pressure could lead law firms themselves to drive ownership and structural reform by 2030.
pts.d: In his own response to discussion of his forecast, he explains that lost market share could push incumbent firms to demand structural change and offer meaningful upside to attract technical talent. This is a conditional prediction, which he calls his 'crazy take'; he does not supply a jurisdiction-specific reform route or explain how licensing and ownership restrictions would be changed. The host's separate prediction of an Uber-style regulatory confrontation is not attributed to Chiriboga.

pts.k: Chiriboga expects legal-service risk tolerance to change as clients weigh imperfect AI against imperfect human work, price, speed and the experience of receiving the service.
pts.d: He suggests that malpractice-driven caution may ease and expresses uncertainty about how strongly clients will demand a human in the loop. This qualifies his broader emphasis on human relationships: he does not present universal lawyer replacement as his forecast. His comparison between human and AI mistakes is experiential argument, not a measured comparison of error or hallucination rates.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies on Chiriboga's professional experience, his account of Nexl's product, personal analogy and speculative market reasoning, rather than systematic empirical evidence.
pts.d: Claim 1 rests on a single recollected discovery experience, without a defined task, quality assessment or independently checked timing. Claim 2 is an executive's description of his company's capabilities, without adoption or outcome metrics. Claim 3 uses legal-practice experience and a personal physical-therapy analogy. Claim 4 is a long-run career forecast with no employment data. Claims 5–6 use comparisons with earlier businesses, an unnamed entrant and reasoning about cost, market share and talent incentives; no market-share figures or regulatory evidence are supplied. Claim 7 invokes his experience as a junior practitioner and human fallibility; no client research, malpractice data or model benchmarks are offered.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims range from a 2015–2016 experience and present-day product descriptions to conditional 2030 market reform and a forty-year career forecast.
pts.d: Claim 1 is dated by Chiriboga to approximately 2015–2016. Claim 2 describes current capabilities at the time of the 2025 interview. Claim 3 has no precise deadline and concerns lawyers who successfully use AI alongside personalised counsel. Claim 4 explicitly looks forty years ahead, approximately 2065 from the interview date. Claims 5–6 depend on an entrant successfully taking substantial market share, incumbent firms feeling threatened, and firms needing technical talent; the reform horizon is 2030, also expressed as five years away. Claim 7 has no specified date and acknowledges imperfect models and uncertainty about demand for human involvement.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Chiriboga identifies effects on practising lawyers, clients, incumbent and technology-led firms, legal-adjacent workers and technical recruits.
pts.d: Discovery lawyers gain task capacity in Claim 1. Lawyers and law-firm business-development functions receive relationship insights with less manual CRM maintenance in Claim 2. Clients and trusted advisers are central to Claim 3's personalised, AI-assisted service model. Legal-career entrants and adjacent professionals gain potential new roles in Claim 4, without any quantified net jobs forecast. Technology-led providers gain potential market share while incumbent firms face competitive pressure in Claims 5–6; engineers become talent that firms may need new compensation or ownership structures to attract. Claim 7 concerns providers' risk attitudes and clients' trade-offs among human involvement, quality, speed and willingness to pay. Chiriboga does not quantify distributional effects or make a specific access-to-justice prediction.
